title: Double Trouble
reviewNotes: Three branches, 20 exact positions from the seven-piece phase after ...Rd2 at 40 seconds. Kf4 and Bd3 double interference compared through both rook captures and a king escape. The d-rook line reaches source Qg5 mate; the c-rook and king-escape lines include independently supplied forced ...Rh2 Rxh2# completions. Source Rh1 mate claim corrected: it is check before the remaining rook block. Earlier eight-piece opening remains source context.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius will be able to find the incredible win that white has in this position. You see, it seems like black is completely winning having a rook for a bishop, but white does have a pawn that is only one step away from getting a new queen. At first glance, it doesn't seem like black can stop this promotion because both of the squares are covered by the bishop, and if the rook tries to come to the back rank, the pawn is going to take it. But, black does have a resilient move with pawn to g2 check. This move forks the rook and the king, so the king has to take the pawn. But, black has lured the king outside so that it can now give a check on e2 and reroute behind the pawn. Now, the bishop has no way of defending the pawn because both of these squares are covered by the rook, but white can continue with a very clever idea. King to f4. This sets up a checkmate threat because the white king is covering all of the escape squares of the black king, and not only that, the bishop is an extension of the wall that the king is creating, meaning that if the black king tries to run this way, this is still going to be a checkmate. And if the black king runs this way, now after this check by the rook, black has to cover. We're going to trade, and then we're going to be able to promote. But, do not celebrate too soon because black can simply play rook to c3 and defend the check with this rook while still covering the promotion square. And now, it might seem like black is simply out of the woods. There is no checkmate, and there is no promotion. But, little did black know that he fell right into our trap after the incredible and brilliant bishop to d3, a sacrifice of an entire bishop. But, this is a double interference. We are stopping the view of the rook that defends the promotion and the view of the rook that defends the checkmate, meaning that if the c rook captures, we are now free to promote safely because if the queen is taken, this is going to be a checkmate. But if the D rook captures, we can now give a check that would be a checkmate. So, black has to cover, and now we can promote to a queen. This is going to lead to a checkmate.
